newsitem.title: KENYA: Somaliland leader backs U.S. plan for peace force.
newsitem.headline: Somaliland leader backs U.S. plan for peace force.

text.p: The President of the self-declared Somaliland Republic on Sunday declared his support for a U.S.-backed plan to set up an African intervention force, and joined the U.S. in opposing the re-election of UN Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali.

In a statement faxed to Reuters from Hargeisa, the Somaliland capital, Mohamed Ibrahim Egal expressed "astonishment" that South African President Nelson Mandela had opposed the US moves in discussions last week with Secretary of State Warren Christopher.
Egal described the peace force proposal as "one of the great hopes for Africa to solve its civil wars and arrest the chaos and the anarchy which is spreading like wildfire."
He added: "To cast a doubt on the need for such a force conveys, at least to me, an abysmal ignorance of the dilemma of the continent of Africa."
Mandela said he could not support such a force unless it was set up through the United Nations.

Egal said President Mandela was wrong in suggesting that Egypt's Boutros-Ghali was the Organisation of Africa Unity's (OAU) choice for UN Secretary-General. "He was not -- he was a compromise candidate," he added.
The Somaliland leader said his country had suffered "untold misery" as a result of the Secretary-General's "arrogant authoritarian decisions.
"History will judge Boutros-Ghali's record in Somalia, former Yugoslavia, Afghanistan and Iraq as the darkest pages in the history of this great international organisation," he added.
"It will be a disservice to the international community and to the UN which represents them to allow Ghali to continue his bungling during the crucial years ahead of us.
"I call on the OAU and the African presidents to contradict President Mandela and affirm Africa's need for a peace force, and to accept the proposal of the U.S. Government."

Somaliland covers the area of the former British Somaliland which joined with Italian Somalia in 1960 to form the independent Republic of Somalia. It broke away from the southern half of the country in 1991, after the fall of president Mohamed Siad Barre, and declared itself independent.
Egal's government has frequently quarrelled with UN agencies who, he says, have ignored the needs of his people.
